1This went alongside an argument about what forms of class struggle were most effective, the revolutionary potential of different kinds of worker, and how the word ‘proletariat’ should be defined (which is a different question from how worker should be defined). For Bakunin’s views on the peasantry and the so-called destitute proletariat see Bakunin 1973, 253-54; Bakunin 1990, 6-8, 177-78, 198-217; Bakunin 2002, 189-209. For the various meanings of the proletariat in 19th century socialism see Baker 2024.

2A recurring accusation that anarchists and Marxists made against each other was plagiarism. In 1851 Engels told Marx that the mutualist Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, who was the first known person to politically self-identify as an anarchist, had “indubitably lifted” his analysis of the state as an instrument of class rule that will disappear with the resolution of class contradictions from the Communist Manifesto and perhaps Marx’s articles in the press (MECW 38, 435). In an amusing twist of fate, Proudhon himself believed that parts of Marx’s The Poverty of Philosophy plagiarised ideas without credit from the very book it was critiquing, namely Proudhon’s System of Economic Contradictions. He wrote in the margins of Marx’s book, “Does Marx have the pretentiousness to claim all of this as his own, in opposition to something contrary which I am supposed to have said?”, “But all that it is me!”, “Plagiarism of my first chapter”, “What! Come on now! But the preceding pages are copies of my own” (Quoted in McKay, 2017). Decades later in the early 1900s the Georgian anarchist Varlam Cherkezishvili accused Marx and Engels of having plagiarised the Communist Manifesto from an earlier book by the French socialist Victor Considerant (Cherkezishvili 1902, 55-66). This claim was then repeated by other anarchists like Malatesta (Malatesta 2023, 213) and Rocker (Rocker 1925).

3Both Marx and Bakunin believed that biological races with different characteristics existed. This was a widespread false belief among biologists at the time. Importantly, Bakunin did not think that what he called moral characteristics, such as cowardice or a commitment to freedom, were biologically heritable and instead credited their transmission to socialisation and life experience. How this process of social development occurs is influenced by prenatal factors, but these generally have a smaller impact than the environment at an individual level. He wrote that, “natural and innate difference, small as it may be, is nevertheless positive and real: difference in temperament, in vital energy, in the predominance of one sense or one group of organic functions over others, difference in vivacity and natural capacities. We have tried to prove that vices as well as moral qualities—facts of individual and social consciousness—cannot be physically inherited, and that man cannot be physiologically predetermined toward evil, nor irrevocably rendered incapable of good. But we have never meant to deny that individual natures differ widely among themselves, that some of them are endowed to a greater extent than others with a capacity for a full human development. True, we believe that these natural differences are now quite exaggerated and that most of them should be attributed not to Nature but to the different education which has been allotted to each individual . . . We have even recognized that in some exceptional cases, in men of genius or of great talent for example, as well as idiots or highly perverse natures, this influence of natural determination upon the development of the individual—a determination as inevitable as the influence of education and society—may be great.” (Bakunin 1964, 153-54). To learn more about Marx’s views on race see Paul 1981. For Bakunin see Bakunin 1964, 147-54; Bakunin 1970, 65-7; Bakunin 1989, 178-79.

4In the appendix to Statism and Anarchy Bakunin made the more plausible argument that the positive aspects of Russia’s peasant communes, which were called the mir, could provide the basis for the emergence of anarchist socialist consciousness in the country. Importantly, he did not think this would occur automatically. He instead emphasised that an organisation of committed revolutionaries had to help forge links between both different peasant communes and between the peasantry and urban workers. He believed that a core goal of this organising should be revolutionaries persuading the peasantry to abandon what he regarded as the three main barriers to them developing anarchist socialist consciousness: patriarchy and faith in the Tsar, alongside the authoritarian tendency of the mir to override individual liberties, be a tool of the state, and a servant of rich peasants (Bakunin 1990, 198-217).

5The following interpretation is indebted to conversations with Paul Raekstad and unpublished drafts he has shown me, alongside my study of Mészáros 2011 and Marx himself.

6Another attendee of the 1865 London conference, the mutualist and later collectivist César De Paepe, used Marx’s critique of Proudhon in polemics with anti-collectivist mutualists. In 1868 he wrote, “thanks to a dialectics put in the service of a method more often metaphysical than scientific (which it is necessary to avoid confusing with the historical and objective method of Karl Marx), Proudhon has discovered in the social world some laws that observation confirms more from day to day; it is, however, incontestable that hypothesis still plays an infinitely more considerable role in the works of that thinker and that often he has concluded a priori or from insufficient observations: witness the conclusions of his last works relative to the social role of strikes and trades-unions, and those relative to the tendencies of modern production towards association and thus towards the collective appropriation of land and the large instruments of labor, two phenomena of which Proudhon has misunderstood the immense scope from the point of view of the organization of the future, and that he condemned even in the name of reason and logic, while Marx, already well before 1848, in the name of observation and history, considers them the two principal elements of the solution of the social problem. The majority of the writers of Liberté have made the defects of Proudhon their own by sacrificing, so to speak absolutely, his scientific side” (De Paepe 2014). It is unclear how De Paepe, who was six when The Poverty of Philosophy was published, acquired knowledge of Marx’s critique of Proudhon. He may have found an old copy of the book. Or perhaps he learnt this information from conversations with Marx and Eccarius at the conference and Marx’s critical obituary of Proudhon, which was published in February 1865 within Der Social-Demokrat (MECW 20, 26-33).

7It is not known how Cafiero first read the Communist Manifesto. One obvious source is Bakunin, who owned a German copy and his own Russian translation of it. Cafiero arrived at Bakunin’s on 20 May 1872 and then read aloud to Bakunin the first part of his letter to Engels on 31 May and the rest on 3 June. It was then sent to Engels on 19 June from Milan, one day after he had left Switzerland (Eckhardt 2016, 223-25). This was enough time in which to read the Manifesto, but I do not know if Cafiero had the required language skills. He definitely read Italian, English, and French to a high level. I have been unable to find evidence that he read German or Russian. This is indirectly supported by the fact that he first read Marx’s Capital in its French translation and not the German original. Bakunin could have read out the Manifesto to Cafiero by translating it in real time as he spoke, but there is no direct evidence that this happened. It has been suggested that the edition of the Manifesto that Cafiero read was the December 1871 English edition published by the American paper Woodhull & Claflin’s Weekly under the title German Communism – Manifesto of the German Communist Party. This is because it would explain why Cafiero referred to the originally titled Manifesto of the Communist Party as the “Manifesto of the German Communist Party” in the letter (Eckhardt 2016, 224, 518n167). Engels had mentioned the publication of this translation in a 15 February 1872 letter to Wilhelm Liebknecht (MECW 44, 319). On 17 March Engels complained to Friedrich Sorge, who lived in the United States, about the quality of the recent translations and asked him to send over “50 copies of the issue of Woodhull & Claflin's which contains the translation of the Communist Manifesto, and 50-100 of the issues of the Socialiste with the French translation” (ibid, 343, 643n440). Engels could have forwarded one of these new copies, or the previous one he owned, to Cafiero. Previously when Engels had sent documents to Cafiero he wrote a letter informing him that they were on their way (ibid, 171). No such letter for the Manifesto has been found. If Engels sent Cafiero a copy it was probably attached to the lost letter that was written between 29 February and 9 March (Eckhardt 2016, 225). It should also be kept in mind that Bakunin referred to the Manifesto as “the famous manifesto of the German Communists” in the unsent October 1872 letter to the editors of La Liberté and his 1873 book Statism and Anarchy (Bakunin 1973, 252; Bakunin 1990, 146). As a result, Bakunin could potentially have also been the reason why Cafiero used this phrase.

8Engels privately complained about this distortion of his and Marx’s ideas in a few letters. See MECW 49, 34-6, 59-63, 197; MECW 50, 163-65, 264-67.

9It is unclear why this is the case. In the preface they claim that “the present memoir, ‘God and the State,’ is really a fragment of a letter or report. Composed in the same manner as most of Bakunin's other writings, it has the same literary fault, lack of proportion; moreover it breaks off abruptly: we have searched in vain to discover the end of the manuscript” (Bakunin 1970, 6). But this account was later contradicted by Guillaume, who had originally provided Reclus with the relevant manuscripts. He complained in 1908, “that last assertion is incomprehensible to me, for the end of the manuscript (pages 248-340) was found, along with the part published by Reclus and Cafiero, in the case passed by me to Élisée Reclus; that case also contained pages 139-148, which Reclus and Cafiero have not included, a proof of pages 139-148, and a proof of pages 149-210; the second of these proofs bore corrections of style and some deletions in the hand of Reclus and in one other hand; I find it still more difficult to explain, in view of that circumstance, that the editors of 1882 could have called this piece “a fragment from a letter or report.” This little literary artifice — for that is probably what it is — was not necessary to make the reader appreciate the high value of those pages” (Guillaume, 2016).

title: Socialism or Barbarism? - S'bu Zikode
content:
Keynote address by S'bu Zikode, from Abahlali baseMjondolo, at the Third National Conference of the Aotearoa New Zealand Federation of Socialist Societies held in Ōtepoti Dunedin, on Saturday, 14 November 2026.

Comrade Programme director, thank you for welcoming me to Aotearoa once again. May I express my sincere gratitude to the New Zealand Federation of Socialist Societies and Palestine Solidarity Network Aotearoa for inviting me to speak here today, and across the country. I bring greetings from Abahlali baseMjondolo, our movement in South Africa which now has more than 200,000 members.

I want to begin with the words of a song, a song about socialism, that is often sung in the struggles of the left in South Africa.

Yini iSocialism? Umhlaba wonke ezandleni zabantu Akunamuntu, akunamuntu ongaphatha umhlaba ngayedwa Ayayesaba bo, ayesaba amabhujwa, nongxiwa Ngoba bona, ngobabona befuna ukusetshenzelwa ngabantu

The song asks, ‘What is socialism?’ It answers that socialism is the whole world in the hands of the people. It goes on to say that no one person can own the world on their own. It concludes that the bourgeoisie are afraid of socialism, because they want the people to work for them.

Comrades, as you will all know, in 1915, during the mass slaughter of the First World War, Rosa Luxemburg wrote from a prison cell in Germany that humanity stood at a crossroads. Either it would move towards socialism, towards global justice and peace, or it would collapse into further barbarism. She was writing as millions of workers were being sent to kill each other in the trenches for the profits of their rulers. Four years later she was murdered.

In our movement we have our own version of this choice. Lindokuhle Mnguni, the gifted young chairperson of one of our branches, the eKhenana Commune in Durban, introduced the slogan ‘Socialism or Death’ into our movement. For Lindokuhle, socialism was not something that would come one day in the future, after a revolution, or after an election. Socialism had to be lived now, in the way we occupy land, ensure that it is not bought and sold, manage it democratically, grow food together, ensure that nobody goes hungry, care for each other, build and manage social infrastructure like halls, creches and kitchens, and make decisions together.

For us, like urban and rural movements elsewhere in the world, building socialism from below means building communes, connecting them and building wider forms of democratic popular power from these communes. In the same way that the liberated zones were the bases for anti-colonial movements in countries like Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau, communes – from South Africa to Brazil, Venezuela and elsewhere – are the strongest bases for our movements to build socialism. As Ruthie Wilson Gilmore says, ‘Freedom is a place’.

The price for challenging oppression can be very high. Many comrades around the world have given their lives. On 20 August 2022, Lindokuhle was shot dead in his home. He was the third leader of the eKhenana Commune to be assassinated in less than six months.

Frantz Fanon taught that ‘Each generation must, out of relative obscurity, discover its mission, fulfill it, or betray it.’ Comrades like Rosa Luxemburg and Lindokuhle Mnguni understood the mission of their generation, and gave their lives to it. Our generation also has a mission. We are living in a time of genocide, of wealth beyond imagination for a few and hunger for millions, of the far right and fascist forces rising and of the poor being turned against each other. We have to decide whether we will fulfil our mission or betray it. In our movement we have often used Fanon’s words. When people find themselves pushed to the margins of the city and of life, they have the opportunity to discover their mission and to decide whether they want to fulfil it or betray it.

I want to speak today about the barbarism that we see around us, in South Africa and around the world, and about the work of building socialism from below, as we have tried to do it in our movement.

When Luxemburg wrote about barbarism she was thinking of the slaughter of the First World War. Today we are witnessing another mass slaughter of human beings. We have all watched the genocide in Gaza. We have watched children being starved, hospitals and schools being bombed, and whole families being buried under the rubble of their homes. We have watched the most powerful governments in the world supply the weapons and protect Israel at the United Nations. We have watched the liberal governments of the West back Israel and turn on their own citizens when they have stood up for truth and justice. In the United Kingdom, Peter Hallward, a comrade who stood up for us when we were facing violent repression from the ANC in 2009, was arrested and charged with terrorism for holding up a placard at a demonstration in solidarity with the Palestinian people.

There are many kinds of barbarism. We must not hesitate to say that the economic system – capitalism – that makes the rich to be rich and the poor to be poor is barbaric. In January this year it was reported that the wealth of the world’s billionaires had reached 18.3 trillion US dollars, the highest level in history. Their wealth grew by 2.5 trillion dollars in 2025 alone. That increase in one year is almost equal to all the wealth of the poorest half of humanity, more than four billion people. At the same time nearly half of the people in the world live in poverty, and one person in four does not regularly have enough to eat. There are now more than 3,000 billionaires.

This world in which a few thousand people own more wealth than billions of others was made, and it is maintained by force. In our movement we say that we were made poor so that others could be made rich, and that we are kept poor so that others can remain rich. This is why we insist on a world in which land, wealth and power are shared, a world in which every person counts as a person.

In South Africa we won our democracy in 1994. But the poor are now greater in number, and poorer, than they were in 1994, while the rich have become richer and richer. Millions of people still live in shacks. Youth unemployment is at 60% and millions of young people have never had a job. When people organise to demand land, housing and dignity they are evicted, arrested and sometimes killed. Twenty-six of our comrades have lost their lives in the course of our struggle. Some were murdered by the police. Some were murdered by hired killers working for local politicians. Two ANC councillors are serving life sentences for the murder of our comrade Thuli Ndlovu, who was shot dead in her home in 2014 while she was helping a child with homework.

There is another kind of barbarism that comes when the poor and the working class are turned against each other. Everywhere in the world the oppressed are being divided. Xenophobia is the greatest weapon unleashed against the oppressed, but we are also divided by race, by religion in some countries, as well as by language, culture and ethnicity.

The system needs us to believe that our neighbours are taking our jobs and our houses. It needs us to look down at people who are as poor as we are rather than up at the people who are getting rich from our suffering. The crisis in our hospitals is caused by austerity, mismanagement and corruption. There is mass unemployment because we have an economy that was built on extraction and exclusion and that has never broken with its colonial origins.

This is not only a South African problem. Across the world right-wing forces are scapegoating migrants for the devastation caused by capitalism. We see it in Europe. We see it in the United States, where migrants are being hunted by ICE. In South Africa some of the parties that gained votes in our recent local government elections are extremely hostile to migrants. Some of these same parties support Israel. In India Muslims are made into the enemy. In Europe and the United States it is migrants and refugees. In South Africa it is people from Asia and other African countries, and increasingly South Africans who speak minority languages. Each time, the people who are made into enemies are as poor as the people who are told to hate them. Each time, the people who own the land, the mines, the banks and the media are left untouched. Each time the politicians who steal from the people are left untouched. In 2020 we ended a statement against xenophobia with the words Sazi isitha sakho, know your enemy.

To resist this division, and to build the unity of the oppressed, the working class and the poor, is one of the most urgent tasks of our time. Without that unity there can be no socialism.

Today even people who see themselves as workers move between being employed and being impoverished. This is why the unity of the working class and the impoverished is necessary if we are to win the battle against the forces that we are all against. Fanon wrote that when the people come to understand their situation they realise that everything depends on them, and that their salvation lies in their own unity and courage, in the true understanding of their interests and in knowing who their enemies are. For our movement this work of building togetherness begins with the recognition of the humanity of every person. There is only one human race. A person is a person wherever they find themselves. A neighbour is a neighbour and a comrade is a comrade wherever they may come from. Our humanity cannot be judged by where we were born, by the language that we speak or by how much money we have.

Dignity is the ethical core of our politics. The dignity of human beings is universal and non-negotiable, and it is the point from which resistance is built. When we diminish or vandalise the humanity of others we disgrace our own humanity. Hatred of this kind always weakens the poor and the working-class people, and so it has to be rejected by poor and working-class people first.

In May 2008 a wave of xenophobic violence spread across South Africa. At least 62 people were killed and more than 100,000 were driven from their homes. Our movement held a careful discussion over two days, and on 21 May we issued a statement. We said that there is only one human race. We said that an action can be illegal, but a person cannot be illegal. We said, in isiZulu, Unyawo alunampumulo, that a person is a person wherever they may find themselves. We sheltered and defended people who were under attack.

Before 2008 we had spoken a great deal about the dignity of our own members. In 2008 we had to affirm that we were committed to the dignity of everyone.

In 2025 the courts found that Operation Dudula, an organisation that had been blocking migrants from hospitals and attacking them in the streets, was acting in a way that was unlawful and unconstitutional. Operation Dudula is a violent, fascist organisation that uses military uniforms. When they marched on the offices of the Socio-Economic Rights Institute in Johannesburg, the law firm that has represented our movement and many migrants, hundreds of our members stood on the streets to defend the Socio-Economic Rights Institute. When Operation Dudula arrived, they found themselves vastly outnumbered by our members, and they left. Every human being is called to resist fascism and there can be no socialism that is not also anti-fascist.

This year there has been a terrible new wave of organised xenophobic violence in South Africa. In KwaZulu-Natal armed mobs have gone from house to house driving people from their homes, businesses and workplaces. They say that they are just demanding that the laws against illegal migration are enforced but they have repeatedly and openly attacked documented migrants too, including refugees. More than 150,000 people were forced out of the country in a few weeks. As our General Secretary, Thapelo Mohapi, has warned, this kind of violence always starts with the outsider and ends with the minority at home. What we are witnessing has a name and that name is fascism. We draw a line, a red line, against fascism when we insist that every person is a person no matter who and where they are. In 2020, when I spoke to the United Nations Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, I said that our politics needs to develop a living communism, a politic in which every person counts as a person and the dignity of every human being is respected.

Ubuntu, ubuhlalism and socialism

Our own movement was born out of a struggle to be counted as human beings. For years we had been told that we were free, but we did not count in this society. We were not recognised as human beings. Our suffering did not count as human suffering. Our lives did not count as human lives.

Our movement was born in 2005 in a shack settlement called Kennedy Road in Durban. We had been promised land near our settlement for housing. Then we discovered that the land had been sold to a businessman for a brick factory. In March 2005 we blockaded a main road, and many of us were beaten and arrested. We realised that if we wanted to be counted as human beings, we would have to organise ourselves.

From the beginning we insisted that the poor can think for ourselves, speak for ourselves and organise for ourselves. Neighbouring communities saw that our demands were their demands, and they joined us. Together we built a politics of the poor, a homemade politics that everyone can understand and find a home in. We decided that we would think and speak for ourselves and not be told what to do by politicians, by the ruling party or by NGOs. Our meetings were, and remain, open to everyone. Leaders are elected, they must remain accountable to the people, and they can be recalled. A leader is a tool of the people. For our oppressors the people are the tools of the leaders. Our first battles were to defend our settlements from eviction and to win basic services. Over time, as the state destroyed our homes and refused to give us land, we began to occupy unused land ourselves. This is land reform from below, urban planning from below. Land and dignity became central commitments in our movement.

In South Africa we speak of ubuntu, the idea that umuntu ungumuntu ngabantu, a person is a person through other people. It is not often admitted that ubuntu has not always been intended to apply to all people. We have radicalised ubuntu by insisting that it applies to every human being everywhere. For us ubuntu is a practice that demonstrates, builds and defends our shared humanity. In our communities, when a family fell on hard times, another family would lend them livestock. This is what ubuntu meant in practice.

In 2012 our movement spent a whole day in discussion about socialism and communism. Many of us were drawn to these ideas. But socialism often came to us through small sectarian organisations and NGOs, and communism through the South African Communist Party, which is part of the ruling alliance, which was silent while we were being oppressed and is now working with xenophobic and corrupt forces. It seemed to us that both were leaving us out. So, we decided to give our own name to our politics. We called it ubuhlali, the politics of abahlali, the residents, and we rooted it in ubuntu. We spend a great deal of time in our political education on ubuntu, because unless we are responsible human beings who love our fellow human beings, we will not win the battle for justice and equality. This is the most important part of our work, and it comes before we engage in our struggles for land, housing and dignity. We have also spoken of a living politic, a politics that everyone can understand and take part in, that comes from our lives and does not belong to experts. Later we began to speak of a living communism, a communism that emerges from the lives and struggles of the oppressed.

Our road to socialism began with ubuntu. Ubuntu led us to ubuhlali, and ubuhlali led us to democratic socialism from below. It is important to understand that we did not come to humanism from socialism, it was the other way around. We came to socialism from humanism, from the insistence that every human being must count as a human being.

Later we found that in 1844 the young Karl Marx wrote that ‘communism … equals humanism’. In 1960 Léopold Sédar Senghor, the poet who became the first president of Senegal, said, ‘Our socialism is a humanism.’ For us the political form that humanism must take is socialism, and our socialism must always remain a humanism.

When I spoke on UnFreedom Day in 2018 I said that we are struggling for [i]umbuso we socialism lapho wonke umhlaba, nomnotho wezwe uzolawulwa ngabahlali nabasebenzi[i], a socialist order in which all the land and all the wealth of the country will be controlled by the residents and workers.

We have learnt that if you begin with a debate about capitalism and socialism in the abstract you can confuse people on the ground. Politics starts with the everyday lives of people. So, we begin with what people are living, with homelessness, with land and food, with the lack of water and electricity, and with the way that people are treated by the police and by the councillors. When people ask why a family in a middle-class suburb can have seven taps in one house while thousands of us share a handful of toilets, the discussion about racism, political betrayal and capitalism has already begun. Then we can explain the system, how the system of private property degrades the lives of millions to benefit a few. You have to start with what people understand and then build the theory together. You can have brilliant ideas, but if they are detached from the people, they will make no difference to the world.

Rosa Luxemburg understood this. In December 1918, a few weeks before she was murdered, she wrote that the transformation of society ‘cannot be decreed by any bureau, committee, or parliament. It can be begun and carried out only by the masses of people themselves.’ The people, she said, must ‘bring socialism step by step into life’. This is why we say that we are a socialist organisation committed to building socialism from below through the construction of popular democratic power.

When ideas come from the people, are discussed, thought through and returned to the people, they can become very powerful. In 2019, thousands of our members marched through Durban to demand the total decommodification of land. For many years our members had been saying umhlaba noma ukufa, land or death, and many have given their lives in the struggle for land. This demand for the total decommodification of land came out of months of discussion in our branches. We said that land is not a commodity. Land must be allocated on the basis of human need rather than private profit, and it must be managed collectively and democratically by the people who live on it. The social value of land must come before its commercial value.

People sometimes ask us where our socialism comes from. It comes from our lives, from thinking about our lives together, although some of us have also read many books.

Our movement was formed on 4 October 2005 at a meeting of 32 people. Today we have more than 200,000 members. Over the last twenty-one years we have learnt some things about how to build a movement. I would like to share some of these things in case they are useful.

There is no emancipatory politics without listening to others. To lead people is to listen to them, because the people will tell you what to do. When our comrades go to a new community to run political education, they do not bring a programme. They go to listen, to hear what the comrades want to learn. When there is a crisis, we hold assemblies and we listen to everyone, very carefully, before we take a position. Every time you listen to another person you have the opportunity to learn from them. We build our humanity through listening.

A movement must also recognise and support the humanity of its own members now, while it struggles for a world in which the humanity of everyone is recognised. When people come to us the first questions are whether they will be respected and how they will be respected. We come together to develop and defend our humanity and our dignity, and to make the world more human. Our meetings are open to everyone and everyone can speak. When a comrade is sick, we visit them. When a comrade is killed, we bury them with the dignity that they were denied in life. A person who is suffering needs to know that they are not alone. A movement that does not treat its own members as human beings cannot build a more human world.

Building a movement takes courage. Courage has to be built together and sustained together. We must encourage each other.

Building a movement also takes healing. In South Africa we all come out of a history of serious violence, from colonialism and apartheid, to the civil war in KwaZulu-Natal, to the repression that we face today. Other countries have their own histories of oppression and suffering. Without an honest conversation about how to heal together, we will remain unable to build a human form of politics.

Perhaps our most important achievement has been to change the way that people think about themselves. The state creates dependency and division in order to control people. We have built trust and solidarity among the poor; we have built the confidence of the oppressed. When people know that they can resist and win, even if the victories are small, it changes everything.

Leaders must be humble; they must take the ideas of the people seriously and they must remain accountable. When you have to speak for people you have to do justice to the people. Sometimes it is better to be wrong with the people than to be right without the people.

Communities must own the movement, not the leadership. When leaders begin to feel entitled to money or to the assets of the movement, the movement must be strong enough to stop them.

A movement must also protect its autonomy. A movement that gives up its autonomy to a political party or an NGO will quickly collapse.

But autonomy does not mean isolation. No movement can win on its own. It is very important for movements to work with other movements, and with progressive churches, trade unions, lawyers and intellectuals, on the basis of equality and mutual respect.

We have marched with trade unions, with street traders and with organised migrants. Today we stand with the South African Federation of Trade Unions in taking a principled line against xenophobia.

We have had wonderful relationships with some academics, who have worked with us with humility and respect for many years, and good relationships with many progressive organisations of different kinds. But we have also had very bad and damaging experiences with some academics and NGOs. Some of them thought that their role was to think for poor people. This included liberals, and also the kind of leftists who see their role as giving political direction to the oppressed rather than working with the oppressed on the basis of mutual respect. When we insisted on taking our direction from our own members some of them became openly hostile to us. When we refused to be treated as people who cannot think, some said that someone else must be thinking for us, that we were being controlled from behind. This is a very old racist idea about black people who struggle for their freedom. It has done great damage to the left in South Africa, and we sometimes hear about the same kind of thing in other countries.

Mutual respect is the only basis on which a powerful left can be built. Unity between movements and other organisations must be built in cities, in countries and across the world. We are part of a global movement of movements and always work to build internationalism. Some people are surprised when they come to our meetings and hear how beautifully our choir sings the Internationale. They should not be. Internationalism is for all of humanity.

We will end as we began. [i]Yini iSocialism?[i] Socialism is all of the world in the hands of the people. All of us here today, all of us in this room have made the same choice. We have chosen socialism over barbarism. Now our task is to work together to fulfil our mission.

author: Indo
title: On “Sultat al-Majalis”
content:
Rather interesting text on the Arab Council Communist group “Sultat al-Majalis” formed by Lafif Lakhdar and Mustapha Khayati. Originally published in "Al-Hewar Al-Mutamadin, Issue 8699, 6th May 2026”. Can be found here.

The Arab Communist Grouping, which published the magazine Sultat al-Majalis (The Power of Workers’ Councils), was a revolutionary organization that adopted the ideas of council communism, drawing inspiration from the experiences of workers’ councils in Europe. The group was active in the early 1970s and consisted of intellectuals and workers of Maghrebi (North African) origin living in France. Its members were influenced by the events of May 1968 in France and by the left-wing critique of the existing socialist regimes of the time.

The group focused on the idea that revolution should be led by workers’ councils elected directly by the workers themselves. It rejected the traditional Leninist party model and centralized bureaucratic authority. It regarded Soviet communism, as well as its Chinese Maoist counterpart, as systems that had nothing to do with socialism. In its view, both were forms of state capitalism, owned and controlled by a new class known as the bureaucracy, which, like the bourgeoisie, was hostile to the working class and its independent movement.

The organization also launched a scathing critique of existing Arab regimes, whether self-proclaimed progressive or conservative, as well as all Palestinian organizations and the very idea of a Palestinian revolution, insofar as it remained detached from an all-encompassing Arab revolution aimed at overthrowing the existing state structures across the various Arab countries.

The first and only issue of Sultat al-Majalis was published in January 1974. Its purpose was to promote awareness of the self-organization of workers and peasants, free from the tutelage of political parties. The magazine included translations of texts by leading international theorists of council communism, articles analyzing the Arab-Israeli conflict from a class-based perspective that rejected nationalism, and studies of Arab labor movements.

Despite its limited organizational base, the group had a notable intellectual influence in independent left-wing circles and helped introduce concepts of workers’ self-management. It remains one of the distinctive experiments in the history of the Arab Left, representing an attempt to offer a third alternative outside the frameworks of Arab nationalism and official communism aligned with Moscow.

The group operated clandestinely, which meant that some of its contributors wrote under pseudonyms while others remained behind the scenes. Its initial core included young university graduates from Beirut who had been influenced by the global New Left movement but chose to work under the umbrella of the group in order to distinguish themselves from the official communist parties and the Organization of Communist Action in Lebanon.

The relationship between Lafif Lakhdar (1934–2013) and Mustapha Khayati was central to the establishment of this tendency. In his writings, Lafif Lakhdar confirmed that he and Mustapha Khayati had overseen the publication of Sultat al-Majalis.

Mustapha Khayati was a Tunisian activist and intellectual, a prominent member of the Situationist International in France, and the author of the famous pamphlet On the Poverty of Student Life. Khayati brought Situationist thought and the critique of the “Society of the Spectacle” into the Arab context, an influence that was reflected in the pages of Sultat al-Majalis.

Lafif Lakhdar was a radical left-wing Tunisian intellectual and one of the most outspoken critics of state capitalism in the Soviet Union and the Arab regimes. He argued that the genuine alternative lay in the “power of workers’ councils,” exercising self-management. This position formed the central ideological identity of the group.

The magazine served as a platform through which Khayati and Lakhdar translated unorthodox Marxist texts and analyzed Arab conflicts from an internationalist perspective.

Regarding the joint activities of three members of the group in early 1970, before its formal establishment, the Palestinian journalist Bilal al-Hassan wrote the following in an article discussing the book Nayef Hawatmeh Speaks, published in Beirut in 1997:

“... After the name of the Democratic Front [for the Liberation of Palestine] became widely known, along with its Marxist orientation, large numbers of Arab and foreign Marxists and communists began joining its ranks.

Among the most prominent figures who joined the Front at the time were three individuals distinguished by their extensive Marxist knowledge and familiarity with the European critical debate on Soviet Marxism: Lafif Lakhdar (Tunisia), Mustapha Khayati (Tunisia), and Hakima Barada (Morocco).

These three engaged extensively with the Democratic Front and spent time with its cadres and fighters in their military bases. They also proposed establishing a school for cadres, developed its educational curriculum, and participated in the educational process.

The three adopted the Marxism of Rosa Luxemburg as the foundation for educating the Front's cadres. They explained the theory of popular councils to these cadres at length, with their explanations ultimately leading to a critique of Lenin's theory of the party.

This experiment came to an end only when a member of the leadership visited the school and raised the issue before the Political Bureau, criticizing and warning against it.

These examples make it clear that what was known as the Marxism of the Democratic Front was subject to competing ideological currents, reflecting a state of intellectual disarray within the Front, concealed beneath an exceptionally vibrant and energetic political environment...”

(Al-Safir, Lebanese newspaper, February 24, 1998.)

In April 2026, in response to a request from an editor at the electronic website Matzpen, Mustapha Khayati provided the following details about the prominent activists in the group:

“The Sultat al-Majalis group consisted of a small circle of intellectuals who worked for a living. We had nothing beyond what we earned through our own labor.

Here are the names of our comrades:

Hakima Barada: A student working toward her doctorate. I used to share with her what I earned from writing for some obscure encyclopedias. She came from a well-known family that had fallen on hard times, forcing her brothers and sisters to find work in various service-sector occupations.

Kamal Lhbabi: An architect who refused to practice his profession even for a single day. Instead, he learned the craft of pottery and continued working as a potter until he developed kidney failure, from which he still suffers. He was born in 1946 and, like Hakima, was Moroccan.

Saleh al-Mathlouthi: At the time of Sultat al-Majalis, he was teaching in French secondary schools after graduating from the Faculty of Law. He is the father of the singer Emel Mathlouthi, known for her revolutionary songs in three languages: Arabic, French, and English.

Mohamed Chaïrat: At the time, he was working in factories. He later became an Arabic-language teacher and translator. He passed away several years ago.

Najib Ayad: A fellow factory worker alongside Chaïrat. He fled Tunisia with him during the Bourguiba era, subsequently completed his education, and returned to Tunisia under Ben Ali, where he worked at one of its universities. He was the cause of a disagreement between Lafif and me. He was the first among us to pass away.

That, in brief, was the Sultat al-Majalis contingent.

After years of estrangement, I met Lafif in Cairo while I was working as the director of a library at a French research center. We greeted one another warmly, bringing the estrangement to an end and restoring our friendship, although it was never quite what it had been before.

The group ceased to exist in 1976, and the revolutionary tide came to an end as well. Hakima and I returned to Morocco, where I stayed for ten years before moving to Aix-en-Provence to teach the history of political thought in the Islamic world.”

This is Mustapha Khayati's account.

Because of their ideological affinity, connections developed in Europe between members of the Sultat al-Majalis group and the Israeli socialist organization Matzpen.

During the October 1973 War, the two organizations signed a joint statement, which was published in both Sultat al-Majalis and Matzpen magazines.

The magazine Sultat al-Majalis also published an article by Lakhdar calling for dialogue with Matzpen.

In early May 1976, revolutionary socialists from several Arab countries and Israel, including members of both Matzpen and the Sultat al-Majalis groups, met and issued a joint appeal addressed to Arab and Israeli workers and revolutionary youth. It was entitled:

“No to War, Yes to Proletarian Revolution!”

Matzpen published the appeal in its bulletin, From Our Struggle Against Zionism and for Socialism.

author: rezgar2
title: نحو أممية يسارية رقمية في مواجهة الرأسمالية الرقمية، اليسار الرقمي في زمن الخوارزميات
content:
إن المعركة حول التكنولوجيا هي أيضاً معركة حول الملكية والسلطة والوعي ومستقبل البشرية. ومع اتساع دور الفضاء الرقمي بوصفه إحدى الساحات الرئيسية للصراع الطبقي، يمكن للأممية اليسارية الرقمية أن تصبح نقطة انطلاق لتجديد العمل الأممي عموماً. ويتمثل التحدي اليوم في البناء على التشخيص بأدوات جماعية للمواجهة، وفي تطوير التعاون العملي القائم بين قوى اليسار وتوسيعه، ليكمل المواقف والبيانات التضامنية بعمل مشترك أكثر تنظيماً واستمرارية، وفي التوجه التدريجي من منصات الاحتكارات إلى بدائل مستقلة وديمقراطية. وبذلك يمكن أن تتحول إمكانات الثورة الرقمية من امتياز تستأثر به حفنة من الشركات والدول الكبرى إلى مكسب عام يخدم الإنسان وتحرره.

صدر حديثاً كتاب «نحو أممية يسارية رقمية في مواجهة الرأسمالية الرقمية، اليسار الرقمي في زمن الخوارزميات» نصوص ودراسات وبرنامج عمل حول اليسار الرقمي والأممية اليسارية الرقمية، من إعدادي وتأليفي، وهو متاح إلكترونياً ومجاناً.

يشهد العالم ثورة رقمية متسارعة تعيد تشكيل الاقتصاد والعمل والسياسة والوعي الإنساني. وفي الوقت الذي تفتح فيه هذه الثورة إمكانات هائلة للتقدم والتحرر البشري وتجاوز الفقر والأمراض، تتركز ملكية أدواتها ومواردها الأساسية في أيدي حفنة من الاحتكارات الرأسمالية المدعومة من الدول الكبرى. وفي المقابل، تتسع الاحتجاجات الجماهيرية والشبابية في كثير من بلدان العالم، مستفيدة من الأدوات الرقمية في التنظيم والتعبئة، ومؤكدة أن الظروف الموضوعية لتجاوز الرأسمالية قائمة.

ومن هذا التناقض تنبع الحاجة إلى مسار متكامل يبدأ بفهم الرأسمالية الرقمية، ويمر بإغناء تجربة اليسار فكرياً وتنظيمياً بما يواكب التطورات الراهنة، وصولاً إلى بناء أممية يسارية رقمية قادرة على التأثير.

تتيح الثورة الرقمية تقليص ساعات العمل، وتطوير الخدمات الصحية والتعليمية، وتحرير الإنسان من الأعمال المرهقة والمتكررة. غير أن هذه الإمكانات تتطور في إطار علاقات إنتاج رأسمالية، تستحوذ فيها الاحتكارات على القسم الأكبر من مكاسب التقدم التكنولوجي.

فالخوارزميات والمنصات الرقمية ليست محايدة اجتماعياً أو طبقياً، إذ تتأثر بعلاقات الملكية والتمويل والإدارة. وتتجاوز هذه الهيمنة حدود الاقتصاد إلى تشكيل الوعي وتوسيع المراقبة وتوظيف التكنولوجيا في القتل والحروب، ويزيد تقارب بعض قوى اليمين المتطرف مع الاحتكارات التكنولوجية من مخاطر الفاشية الرقمية.

وأمام هذا الواقع، يبرز السؤال الجوهري: كيف يقاوم اليسار الرأسمالية في طورها الرقمي المتقدم، ويفتح الطريق نحو بديل اشتراكي إنساني أكثر عدلاً، محلياً وعالمياً؟ وكيف يجدد نفسه ويطورها ليكون قادراً على ذلك؟

فقد أصبحت الرأسمالية الرقمية قوة عابرة للحدود، بينما يبقى جزء كبير من العمل اليساري الرقمي محصوراً داخل الأطر الوطنية، ويعاني ضعف التنسيق الرقمي الأممي. وتكشف التجارب الحديثة حجم الخطر الذي يواجهه اليسار في هذا الميدان.

ففي البرازيل، وخلال سباق رئاسي بالغ التقارب عام 2026 بين لولا دا سيلفا ومرشح اليمين المتطرف فلافيو بولسونارو، اتهم لولا وحزبه شركة ميتا بتقليص انتشار منشوراته لمصلحة خصمه. وتدخلت المحكمة الانتخابية العليا وألزمت الشركة بتقديم توضيحات، ونشرت صحيفة «فولها دي ساو باولو» مراسلات داخلية يقر فيها موظفون في الشركة بأن قيود المنصة أضرت بحسابات لولا، فيما تحدثت ميتا عن «أعطال تقنية». ورغم ذلك، حسمت التعبئة الجماهيرية جولة الإعادة لصالح لولا.

وفي ألمانيا، وظّف إيلون ماسك منصته «إكس» لدعم حزب «البديل من أجل ألمانيا» اليميني المتطرف قبيل انتخابات فبراير 2025، عبر مقالات التأييد وبثّ حوار مباشر مع زعيمته أليس فايدل، فيما رصدت دراسات انحياز خوارزميات المنصة لصالح محتوى الحزب. وفي كولومبيا، وبعد جولة إعادة حسمت لمرشح اليمين المتطرف بفارق نحو نقطة مئوية واحدة، اتهم الرئيس غوستافو بيترو شركة سايبر إسرائيلية بنشر نصف مليون حساب آلي زائف للتلاعب بالناخبين، وطعن في سلامة برمجيات الفرز وانحياز المنصات الرقمية لليمين المتطرف. ومهما انتهى إليه التحقيق، فإن انتقال الطعن في انتخابات بلد بأكمله إلى ميدان الخوارزميات والحسابات الآلية يكشف طبيعة المرحلة التي نعيشها.

أما المثال الأوضح فجاء من المحكمة الجنائية الدولية. فبعد أن أصدر قضاتها مذكرات توقيف بحق مسؤولين إسرائيليين بتهم ارتكاب جرائم حرب في غزة، فرضت الإدارة الأمريكية عقوبات على عدد من قضاتها ومسؤوليها، فأغلقت شركات أمريكية حساباتهم المصرفية والرقمية. وإذا كانت الرأسمالية مستعدة لفعل ذلك بمحكمة دولية تضم أكثر من مئة وعشرين دولة عضواً، فماذا ستفعل بمشروع يساري يصبح مؤثراً ويسعى إلى كسر هيمنتها، ويتجاوز الخطوط الحمراء التي رسمتها؟

وتمتد هذه الهيمنة إلى الحياة اليومية للناشطات والناشطين، عبر عقوبات رقمية تفرضها المنصات على من يفضح جرائم الحرب الإسرائيلية وانتهاكات دول أخرى، أو يطرح خطاباً يسارياً جذرياً. وتبدأ هذه العقوبات بالتضييق وتقليص الانتشار والتهميش، وتصل إلى حذف المحتوى وإغلاق الحسابات. وقد وثقت منظمات حقوق الإنسان الدولية هذه الممارسات وأدانتها، ومنها تقرير «هيومن رايتس ووتش» عن الرقابة الممنهجة على المحتوى الفلسطيني في منصات ميتا. ويدفع هذا القمع الرقمي كثيراً من الناشطات والناشطين إلى رقابة ذاتية طوعية، فيعدلون خطابهم ويتجنبون قضايا بعينها خوفاً من الحظر وإغلاق الحسابات، فتترسخ الهيمنة الفكرية من دون حاجة إلى قمع مباشر.

وتؤكد هذه التجارب صعوبة مواجهة احتكارات رأسمالية تتحكم بالمنصات والبيانات والبنية التحتية والذكاء الاصطناعي بجهود محلية متفرقة، خاصة أن قوى الرأسمالية تتلاقى، رغم صراعاتها التنافسية، في الدفاع عن المصالح الطبقية العامة لرأس المال.

ومن هنا يطرح على اليسار سؤال ثان محدد وواضح: كيف تخوض قوى التغيير معركة سياسية على أرض يملك الخصم الطبقي بنيتها التحتية ويضع قواعد الظهور عليها؟ فمن يخوض معركته على منصات يملكها غيره، يدخل مباراة حكمها منحاز، وتكشف شواهد متعددة كيف يمكن توظيف قواعد هذه المنصات وخوارزمياتها في خدمة مصالح سياسية وطبقية محددة، وفي دعم قوى اليمين المتطرف.

من هذين السؤالين ينطلق مشروع اليسار الرقمي، مستنداً إلى التراث الاشتراكي، وفي مقدمته الماركسية بوصفها منهجاً تحليلياً حياً. فكما حلل ماركس وإنجلز رأسمالية عصرهما بأدوات زمنهما، واستفادا من أحدث ما توصلت إليه العلوم في عصرهما، تقع على اليسار اليوم مهمة تحليل الرأسمالية الرقمية وأشكال استغلالها الجديدة، مستفيداً من العلوم والتقنيات الرقمية الحديثة في تجديد فكره وتنظيمه وأدوات نضاله. فمواجهة رأسمالية تجدد نفسها باستمرار تتطلب يساراً يجدد نفسه أيضاً.

ويتطلب ذلك تجديداً فكرياً يدرس أشكال العمل والاستغلال الجديدة، ويغني مفاهيم الطبقة والملكية والسلطة في ضوئها. ويرافقه تطوير تنظيمي يوسع المشاركة الجماعية، ويعزز ما تراكم من تقاليد القيادة الجماعية وتداول المواقع القيادية والشفافية، ويستفيد من الأشكال التنظيمية الأكثر مرونة وأفقية، ومن أشكال مختلفة ومتدرجة من العضوية تفتح المجال أمام طاقات أوسع للإسهام في العمل اليساري. ويعزز هذا التطوير حضور النساء والشباب في مواقع القرار، ويوسع مساحة المبادرة أمام الشباب، بما يمتلكونه من مهارات رقمية واسعة، للمشاركة الفاعلة في صنع القرار.

ويقوم ذلك كله على التكامل بين النضال الرقمي والعمل الميداني. فالشبكات الرقمية تسرع التنظيم والتعبئة والتضامن، وتكتمل قيمتها حين تتحول إلى حضور فعلي في مواقع العمل والسكن والدراسة وفي الشوارع. ويحتاج ذلك إلى وعي رقمي تقدمي ينقل الأعضاء والجماهير من مجرد استخدام التكنولوجيا إلى فهم آليات عملها والتحكم بها، وإدراك كيف تصمم الخوارزميات لتوجيه الوعي وصناعة القبول.

ويرتبط هذا التجديد بتطوير تقني متواصل، واستخدام فاعل وحذر للأدوات الرقمية في التنظيم والتواصل والتعبئة والديمقراطية الداخلية، من الاجتماعات عن بعد إلى التصويت الإلكتروني وفق ضوابط ديمقراطية وأمنية واضحة، وبتدريب منهجي يشمل كافة المستويات، من الهيئات القيادية إلى القواعد، ويجمع بين الوعي الرقمي الطبقي والأمن الرقمي والمهارات التقنية.

ولحماية هذا المسار من التبعية، تبرز أهمية الاستقلالية اليسارية بركائزها الخمس: السياسية والتنظيمية والمالية والإعلامية والرقمية. وقد أصبحت الاستقلالية الرقمية ركيزة أساسية لحماية الاستقلالية السياسية والتنظيمية والمالية والإعلامية، إذ إن ضعفها يجعل الركائز الأخرى أكثر عرضة للاختراق والتحكم والتقييد، فالتنظيم الذي يعتمد كلياً على منصات الاحتكارات يضع مفتاح إيقافه يوماً ما في يد خصمه الطبقي.

وإذا كان التجديد الفكري والتنظيمي والرقمي ضرورياً لتطوير قدرات اليسار داخل كل بلد، فإن الطابع العالمي للرأسمالية الرقمية، وما تكشفه الوقائع الأخيرة من حجم قدرتها على الفعل، يفرضان الانتقال إلى مستوى آخر من التعاون والتنسيق. لذلك تتضح ضرورة بناء أممية يسارية رقمية فاعلة، بوصفها إحدى الأدوات التنظيمية والنضالية لمواجهة الرأسمالية الرقمية، وجزءاً من النضال الأوسع من أجل التغيير الاشتراكي.

ويأتي البدء بالميدان الرقمي اليوم لأنه أصبح إحدى الساحات الرئيسية للصراع الطبقي والسيطرة على الوعي، في وقت يعاني فيه اليسار نقصاً كبيراً في العمل الرقمي الأممي المشترك. ويقوم هذا المشروع على التعاون الطوعي بين قوى وتيارات يسارية وتقدمية متعددة، مع احترام استقلاليتها وتنوعها. فالاختلافات بين قوى اليسار حقيقية، والتعاون بينها ضروري على أساس نقاط الالتقاء والأهداف المشتركة في هذا المجال. والتاريخ يعلمنا أن الأمميات اليسارية نشأت حين أدرك المنخرطون فيها أن ما يجمعهم أكبر مما يفرقهم، دون انتظار الاتفاق على كل التفاصيل. فقد جمعت الأممية الأولى عام 1864 تيارات متباينة، من الماركسيين واللاسلطويين إلى النقابيين البريطانيين، حول قضية تحرر العمال. ووحدت الأممية الثانية عام 1889 أحزاباً يسارية ونقابات من بلدان عدة، فجعلت الأول من أيار يوماً عالمياً للعمال، وخاضت نضالاً مشتركاً من أجل يوم العمل بثماني ساعات.

ويمكن أن تكون نقطة الانطلاق اجتماعاً أممياً مفتوحاً عبر الإنترنت، تتفق فيه القوى الراغبة على أولويات مشتركة، ثم تتشكل شبكات تنسيق محلية وإقليمية وعالمية، تعمل من خلال لجان وورش عمل دائمة، يتولى كل منها ميداناً محدداً. وعلى هذا الأساس، يمكن طرح خطوات عملية قابلة للتنفيذ التدريجي، من أبرزها:

الاستقلالية الرقمية: إجراء تدقيق رقمي داخل كل تنظيم يحدد حجم التبعية، ثم الانتقال التدريجي إلى بريد وخوادم ومنصات ووسائل اتصال مستقلة ومفتوحة المصدر.

التنسيق والتمويل والكفاءات: بناء شبكة تنسيق لامركزية، وصندوق تمويل جماعي مستقل، وشبكة أممية تجمع الكفاءات التقنية المتفرقة.

التضامن الرقمي: وضع بروتوكول للاستجابة السريعة يساعد التنظيمات المستهدفة بالقمع والحجب والهجمات الرقمية على استعادة أرشيفاتها ومواقعها، ويرافقه ضغط حقوقي وقانوني.

خارطة المبادرات القائمة: رصد المبادرات الرقمية التقدمية الموجودة قبل بناء أي مشروع جديد، لتجنب تكرار الجهود ودعم ما ينجح منها.

التعليم والتدريب: تأسيس منصة تعليمية مفتوحة ومتعددة اللغات والمستويات، تعرف العاملات والعمال بكيفية استخدام الخوارزميات في مراقبة العمل، وبالحقوق التي يمكنهم المطالبة بها.

التطوير التكنولوجي المشترك: إنشاء مختبرات تقنية مشتركة، وتعاونيات رقمية تختبر الملكية الجماعية والديمقراطية للأدوات، بالتعاون مع مجتمعات البرمجيات الحرة.

الإعلام والمعرفة: بناء شبكات للترجمة التعاونية والنشر والأرشفة الرقمية متعددة اللغات.

الحقوق والعدالة الرقمية: تشكيل شبكة قانونية وحقوقية دولية تصوغ مشاريع قوانين نموذجية، وتدعم التقاضي الاستراتيجي لحماية البيانات والخصوصية ومساءلة الاحتكارات.

مناهضة الحروب: إطلاق حملة أممية لتجريم توظيف الذكاء الاصطناعي في الحروب والقتل والقمع، ومساءلة الشركات المتورطة فيه.

العدالة الجندرية: ضمان حضور فعلي للنساء في فرق التصميم والتطوير ومواقع القرار، وتدقيق جندري منتظم للأدوات الرقمية.

البدائل الرقمية: تطوير بدائل تقدمية في البحث والتواصل الاجتماعي والذكاء الاصطناعي، تخضع لإدارة ورقابة ديمقراطيتين.

وتتكامل هذه المسارات مع النضالات العمالية والنسوية والحقوقية. والبداية ممكنة بموارد محدودة، فكل تنظيم أو نقابة أو مجموعة تقنية تستطيع المساهمة وفق إمكاناتها، ومع تراكم المبادرات تتشكل قدرات جماعية أوسع. وهنا يبرز السؤال عن النتائج الممكنة لهذا المسار خلال السنوات الخمس المقبلة.

إذا تلاقت هذه المقترحات في مسار عمل مشترك، يمكن تصور ما قد تحققه الأممية اليسارية الرقمية خلال خمس سنوات، ينتقل فيها التعاون تدريجياً من المحلي إلى الإقليمي ثم العالمي.

في السنة الأولى، يمكن تأسيس شبكات التنسيق وصندوق التمويل وشبكة الكفاءات، وتقييم التبعية الرقمية للتنظيمات المشاركة، وإنجاز خارطة المبادرات القائمة، وإطلاق برامج التدريب والأمن الرقمي، وعقد الجلسات الأولى للملتقى الرقمي الدوري.

في السنة الثانية، يمكن توسيع الشبكات إقليمياً، وإنشاء مختبرات تقنية مشتركة تقدم أدوات تجريبية للتواصل الآمن، وخاصة للناشطات والناشطين في الدول الاستبدادية، وإطلاق المنصة التعليمية، وتشكيل فرق قانونية وحقوقية.

في السنة الثالثة، تخضع هذه الجهود للاختبار العملي. فحين يتعرض تنظيم يساري للقمع أو الحجب، تساعده الشبكة على استعادة أرشيفاته ومواقعه من نسخ احتياطية موزعة على بلدان متعددة. وتظهر نتائج ملموسة للتعاونيات الرقمية، وتتوسع الحملة ضد الاستخدام الحربي والقمعي للذكاء الاصطناعي.

في السنة الرابعة، يمكن أن تظهر نسخ أولية من محركات بحث وشبكات تواصل تقدمية، تقوم على الشفافية وحماية الخصوصية. وتتوسع المنصة التعليمية بلغات متعددة، وتبدأ الشبكة القانونية بانتزاع أحكام تفرض المساءلة على الشركات الاحتكارية.

وفي السنة الخامسة، يمكن أن تتوج هذه الجهود بمشروع إعلان عالمي للحقوق والعدالة الرقمية، وتطوير أدوات ذكاء اصطناعي تعاونية مفتوحة المصدر، وتعزيز مشاركة النساء في بناء التكنولوجيا، وتوسيع التضامن الأممي إلى ميادين العمل والمناخ ومناهضة الحروب.

وهذه التصورات احتمالات عملية مفتوحة للنقاش، تتوقف على الإرادة الجماعية وموازين القوى والإمكانات. ويبقى أثرها الأعمق في تطور الوعي الجماهيري الرقمي.

إن المعركة حول التكنولوجيا هي أيضاً معركة حول الملكية والسلطة والوعي ومستقبل البشرية. ومع اتساع دور الفضاء الرقمي بوصفه إحدى الساحات الرئيسية للصراع الطبقي، يمكن للأممية اليسارية الرقمية أن تصبح نقطة انطلاق لتجديد العمل الأممي عموماً.

ويتمثل التحدي اليوم في البناء على التشخيص بأدوات جماعية للمواجهة، وفي تطوير التعاون العملي القائم بين قوى اليسار وتوسيعه، ليكمل المواقف والبيانات التضامنية بعمل مشترك أكثر تنظيماً واستمرارية، وفي التوجه التدريجي من منصات الاحتكارات إلى بدائل مستقلة وديمقراطية. وبذلك يمكن أن تتحول إمكانات الثورة الرقمية من امتياز تستأثر به حفنة من الشركات والدول الكبرى إلى مكسب عام يخدم الإنسان وتحرره.

ويشرفني كثيراً أن يضم القسم الثاني من الكتاب مساهمات كاتبات وكتاب أعزاء، تناولوا فيها كتابي السابق «الذكاء الاصطناعي الرأسمالي: تحديات اليسار والبدائل الممكنة» الصادر في آذار/مارس 2025، والمقالات التي نشرتها بعده، وهي مساهمة جماعية مهمة في تعزيز الحوار اليساري والتقدمي حول الرقمنة والذكاء الاصطناعي:

مقالات ودراسات بالعربية والكردية: محمد علي مقلد، جاسم سلام عادل، سالم ناصر المهيري، كوران عبد الله، أحمد سلامة، ماجد الشمري، عبد الحميد برتو، طارق فتحي، لوله حميد، ثائر أبو رغيف، هيوا عمر، صباح كنجي، غسان الرفاعي، فواز فرحان، عبده حمد الدوسري، أحمد سليمان، خالد حسين

مقالات ودراسات أجنبية: Alex B. Crane, Sofia Rozlik, Alessandra Ciattini, K. Kaps, Greg Leichner, Burak Görentaş, Özcan Yazıcı, Law and Ethics in Tech

ورتبت الأسماء حسب تاريخ النشر، ومعها العشرات من المعلقات والمعلقين الذين ساهموا في الحوار المفتوح.

وقد استفدت كثيراً من آرائهم ومقترحاتهم ونقدهم في تطوير أفكاري، وأنتهز هذه الفرصة لأجدد لهن ولهم جميعاً خالص الشكر والتقدير، على ما خصصوه من وقت وجهد في القراءة المتأنية والنقاش الجاد.

يتوفر الكتاب على عدد من المنصات العالمية للكتب الإلكترونية، مجاناً أو بسعر رمزي على المنصات التي تشترط التسعير. وقد أكدت تجربة كتابي السابق «الذكاء الاصطناعي الرأسمالي: تحديات اليسار والبدائل الممكنة»، الذي نُشر مجاناً باثنتين وثلاثين لغة، أن النشر الإلكتروني المجاني يوسع دائرة القراء والقارئات من مختلف البلدان، ويفتح باب الحوار على نطاق أوسع، وبالأخص بين شغيلات وشغيلة اليد والفكر من ذوي الدخل المحدود، الذين يصعب عليهم الحصول على الكتب المطبوعة وتحمل كلفتها. وانطلاقاً من قناعتي بأن المعرفة يجب أن تكون مجانية ومتاحة للجميع.

title: Ukraine’s internal aggressor seeks a counteroffensive in the social war: some clarifications for anarchism abroad after the riot near Kiev
content:
There is no fascism in Ukraine. Only a Gestapo, death squads, and a nationwide concentration camp

The activity of our DIY community media depends solely on its audience. Please support our work on this fundraising page for further telling the truth of the streets and the trenches that is forbidden or invisible to the pro-capitalist press. Many thanks everyone!

Following the anti-busification protests that took place over the summer in Kiev and cities in Western Ukraine, the flame of unrest has flared up with renewed intensity. Ukrainian masses have tried to strike back at those who, since 2014, had come to view themselves as an untouchable, sacred caste—a "master race" (on a financial leash of the country’s biggest capitalist, Rinat Akhmetov). Those in Ukraine who had arrogated to themselves the right to speak on behalf of its civil society are now gripped by fear and rage toward those who dared to challenge their monopoly.

A new spark of rebellion flared up on November 2 at 7-A Sunny Street in the village of Petropavlovskaya Borshchagovka (Petropavlivska Borshchahivka). A mobilized man named Andriy Kuleshov had escaped from the 52nd International Assault Regiment "Forge" (military unit 3121)—part of the 1st Corpse of the National Guard "Azov"—and, after his recapture, was held in a private house of this village that had been put up for sale by Sense Bank. According to the unit commander, the unrest began following an attempt to free Kuleshov for $7,000. A 49-year-old plastic surgeon, Valentyna Moloda, arrived at the property in a private ambulance, alleging that men were being held illegally and tortured inside the building. Then, on trial, she stated that she had not intended to incite any provocation; instead, she had come to help persons allegedly being held against their will, acting on a request from a woman who had told her about a man being tortured in an undisclosed location. Moloda denies demanding money for the release of the recruits, maintaining that the sum in question was intended to cover the costs of a private medical evacuation.

One way or other, the statements from TikTok appear to have triggered an unexpected public reaction. A crowd of over a hundred angry people gathered at an NGU deployment site, demanding the release of the men kept hostage there. Some of the protesters claimed to be relatives of those in detention. Military personnel and police subsequently arrived at the scene, and clashes broke out. The crowd rocked a National Guard bus, attempted to break down the gates of the clandestine detention facility, threw eggs and stones at the building’s windows and at the punishers, chanted "Shame!" and "Faggots!" Their vehicles were smashed; someone even used a sledgehammer for this. Tear gas was used against the people. Later, unknown black-clothed ones, wearing balaclavas and carrying wooden bats, appeared on the scene and used force against the protesters. A reporter of the pro-government media outlet UNIAN was also kicked in the stomach by an unidentified person. One of the victims claimed that he and his son were beaten while simply passing by. The NGU stated about 16 militaries injured during deterrence of the crowd.

Then, announces appeared on social media calling on far-right militants to unite for "restoring order" and "responding to outrages" on an ongoing basis. And compelling video evidence of how this went down that evening: "We form a column, four fighters abreast. The question was raised: what if people are waiting for us up ahead—armed, carrying knives? After all, they were the ones who slashed the tires. Did anyone want to step aside? Everyone said, 'We’re going.' We form up and begin to march forward. And we recite the Prayer of the Ukrainian Nationalist: 'Death to the enemies... You shall win freedom or perish in the struggle. Rest assured—you shall not perish; you shall win freedom. I go into battle.' And so, we march, and this... this crowd—I don’t know, it’s like something straight out of a Bosch painting, you know, just all these characters—and for a split second—well, there are these three stages: freeze, run—but for a split second, this crowd of demons (there were hundreds of them) just freezes." We even know whom they are praying to—to the one who needs to reclaim his coal mines and metallurgical plants annexed by Russia…

National Guard Commander Pivnenko and Head of the Presidential Office Budanov arrived at the scene, after which the clashes decreased and people were allowed into the building. The generals officially confirmed that it was a National Guard facility and that men were being held there. The NGU commander stated that the building was rented by "Azov" as a temporary deployment point. According to him, mobilized personnel are taken there after leaving the territorial recruitment centers (TRC), where they undergo "registration and necessary checks" before being sent to training. Servicemen detained after absence without leave (SZCh in Ukrainian) are also being held there. Budanov stated directly that there are many such facilities across Ukraine, explaining this by the mass exodus into SZCh and the need for secrecy to avoid Russian air attacks. Initially, eyewitnesses reported 40 men detained. A woman who was allowed inside with a cop told reporters that she saw about 25-30 people. Later, Pivnenko spoke of 18 servicemen, and Budanov of 14. The information about four injured inmates was confirmed. The recruits admitted that they were indeed in the building and needed medical attention. After the scandal erupted, they were sent to the NGU medical center. Their faces, images of which were shared around the world, show signs of beatings. National Guard spokesman Ruslan Muzychuk, in a comment on the state television channel, stated that the military personnel were sent to one of the medical centers in Kiev region, so that they could receive medical aid.

Along with Valentyna Moloda, a court in Kiev has remanded Tetyana Kireyeva—identified by investigation as the person who "ordered the provocation"—in custody for two months, with no option for bail. According to the prosecutor's office, Kireyeva reached an agreement with Moloda no later than October 30 to coordinate their actions, after which she shared information regarding the location of a military facility via a Telegram group. The following day, an ambulance driver named Viktor Yena—considered an accomplice by investigators—filmed the site and sent the footage to Moloda. In court, Kireyeva explained that she had reached out to Moloda on the advice of her sister, believing that Valentyna—a public figure who heads several private clinics and NGOs, has previously advocated for peace on social media—might be able to help with her husband’s situation. Kireyeva stated that Moloda had offered a service for the "emergency evacuation" of military personnel from TRCs and military units. She confirmed that she had seen the price for this service—107,000 hryvnias—listed in the application. Kireyeva insisted that she had not incited anyone to protest. Here are these brave women — Valentyna on the left and Tetyana on the right:

From the words of Tetyana, she arrived at the building with her two sisters, seeking to have Kuleshov—who she claimed was in critical condition following a beating—admitted to a hospital. "I saved four people. One of them would certainly have died on the 2nd; he wouldn't have made it through the night, as he had a purulent abscess, was covered in ulcers, and there was a horrific stench of pus." She stated that at the "Azov" facility, Kuleshov was beaten on his legs, back, and the back of his head—deliberately avoiding his face to leave no visible marks. Her lawyer presented photographs of Andrey’s injuries to the court. He noted that he had already contacted the State Bureau of Investigation and the Military Prosecutor's Office regarding the beating as early as October 29. According to him, following that report, one of the military servicemen beat Kuleshov again during the night. Kireyeva adds that she had wanted to open the eyes of the "Azov" leadership to what was happening. "I simply wanted to inform the 'Azov' command that there is a specific group using their name as a cover to engage in highly dishonorable conduct. They are bringing shame upon the army." For the fourth suspect, 22-year-old Valeria Ladyka, the court set bail at 66,000 hryvnias. She is accused of blocking a National Guard bus.

A month earlier, Moloda had also posted calls for a pro-peace rally in downtown Kiev. As for the others identified as participants in the unrest, the police and the Security Service of Ukraine are visiting their homes and forcing them to issue apologies. Reportedly, 130 individuals have been identified: 27 took an active part in "unlawful acts," while 24 "behaved aggressively, incited the public, and deliberately provoked conflicts with law enforcement and military personnel." In the best tradition of the Kadyrov regime in Chechnya—probably, when the dictator of Ukraine apologized to Kadyrov, it left such a deep trauma that, to assert himself, he now feels the need to force his own slaves to do the same (much like what happened in Lviv this year summer). There is no word on any charges against those who set up a torture chamber; in today’s Ukraine, such activities are rather rewarded than prosecuted. Just imagine: if it were ever revealed that the 2022 executions in Bucha were actually carried out by the valiant "Azov" warriors, and that it was TRCs staff who were the ones stealing toilets or washing machines—would you really be surprised?

By the end of the week, the military unit officially confirmed that Kuleshov was present there with a stoma—a condition that renders an individual unfit for military service and necessitates his removal from the military register. It remains unclear whether there was an intention to return him to active duty or if he was being held there just for torture.

Following the suppression of the mutiny, the "war to the last poor man" party—speaking out from Kiev offices, TV studios, and rear-echelon military units—is once again demanding harsher criminal penalties for draft evasion, SZCh, and desertion, demanding the use of lethal force against the very people the army supposedly "protects" from Russia, and everything else in their repertoire. Well, we shall see whose teeth are stronger. On one point, at least, Budanov is right: such torture facilities are indeed numerous—in the Kharkov region alone, our team has revealed at least two much larger death camps run by the 225th and the 425th Assault Regiments of the Armed Forces. Regardless of everything, the chronicle of social war is being replenished, including in places far from the capital. Since the possibility of fleeing the country and even of unauthorized leaving one’s military unit is at its lowest point this year since the start of the war.

On October 11, in Sheptytske (Chervonohrad) of the Lviv region, a 47-year-old local man reportedly launched a sudden knife attack, striking a 43-year-old TRC patrolman in the neck during a check of military registration documents. The serviceman sustained a severe injury, including damage to blood vessels and the airway, and was hospitalized in the intensive care unit. The self-defender fled the scene but was soon tracked down by police. During his arrest, he resisted and fired an air pistol in the direction of an cop, wounding him.

On October 12, in the downtown area of Kropyvnytskyi (Kirovohrad), a 53-year-old former military serviceman barricaded himself in an apartment, opened fire on cops with an automatic weapon, and threw a grenade at them. He is a decorated veteran who sustained numerous wounds and concussions during his service. The weapon was seized, and the man has been placed in custody for 60 days without the possibility of bail. The advocate stated that he does not remember some of the events that took place on that evening, although he had not consumed any alcohol.

On the evening of October 19, the flames of a "people’s war" reached the very doorstep of the government quarter: in the Pechersky District TRC in Kiev, an unemployed man who had been busified after being wanted by the TRC wounded three staff members and three policemen with an unregistered handgun. The shooter, named Alexey Kovalsky, was remanded in custody for 60 days by a court on his 42nd birthday. "Our sources state that the suspect was brought to the hearing in a wheelchair—he was unable to move on his own. Kovalsky’s lawyer, Sergey Osyka, claims his client was brutally beaten following his detention. He also notes that Kovalsky surrendered to law enforcement voluntarily after the shooting. According to sources at the medical facility where he is currently being treated, he has sustained a closed craniocerebral injury, a concussion, and a broken nose. Police sources confirm that he was indeed subjected to a rough arrest after the incident. Following the shooting and his subsequent detention, an entire arsenal of weapons was discovered in Kovalsky’s Kiev apartment. He had been walking the streets wearing a bulletproof vest under his clothes and carrying a loaded SigSauer pistol—a model popular among Western special services. Furthermore, his high level of proficiency with the weapon suggests he may have combat experience," reports one of Ukraine’s major political Telegram channels. During busification, no even cursory search was conducted, which allowed Kovalsky to enter the vehicle while already armed. When an attempt was made to search him in the lobby, he drew his weapon and struck six targets with seven shots. A search of his home uncovered smoothbore and automatic weapons, ammunition, and a grenade; he now faces a potential life sentence.

Incidentally, the preventive measure for Kovalsky was determined by "Maidan judge" Andriy Trubnikov. In 2013, he remanded Valeriy Kadura, a participant in the anti-Yanukovich protests, in custody. According to the investigation, Kadura—along with other protesters—drove a bulldozer into law enforcement line near the Presidential Administration building.

Also, on October 19, it was reported that a Kharkov resident had been detained on suspicion of stabbing two members of a "notification group" (or, more accurately, an abduction group) on June 25. The incident resulted in the death of a TRC soldier, who suffered a penetrating stab wound to the heart, while a senior lieutenant was hospitalized with superficial cuts to his head and torso. The suspect is a 50-year-old unemployed man. He had been living with his mother, who chose not to turn him in; instead, she secretly relocated with him to a new place of residence. Operatives identified the locations of the ATMs where the partisan’s mother withdrew cash. At the prosecutor’s request, the detainee has been remanded in custody without the possibility of bail; he faces a sentence ranging from 10 to 15 years, or life imprisonment. The names of both the murdered and the detainee have not been released—partly due to the widespread public jubilation over the death—and remain unknown even to our sources. This is him:

On the evening of October 20, in the community of Tairovo near Odessa, a 44-year-old man stabbed a TRC employee in the neck during a document check. The self-defender was soon apprehended; he now faces up to 15 years in prison on charges of attempted murder…

Meanwhile, the call issued by the Assembly at the beginning of the summer—urging to gather outside Ukrainian embassies to demand freedom for Vadim Kuzub, Hryhorii Kedruk, Andriy Trush, and others imprisoned for reducing the livestock of meat procurers—has turned out to be a voice crying in the wilderness. In these five months, not a single soul abroad has publicly demanded their release. Even mentioning these names, including within Europe’s most radical anti-militarist circles, seems to be a taboo (in these circles, declaring solidarity "with ALL those who refuse to perform military service"—which includes the very "our" head of state, who dodged four draft notices during the Donbass war in 2014–2015—is still considered ultra-revolutionary rhetoric). Nevertheless, as demonstrated by the global campaign launched in August by the Socialist Equality Party in support of Bogdan Syrotiuk, even the most widespread response to our appeal would be unlikely to cause their release. Consider the case of a peaceful Trotskyist author who, on August 10, was sentenced to 15 years in prison solely just for expressing internationalist views in his writings: when thousands of people from various countries showed solidarity by signing petitions and sending emails to the court, the response was like "We do as we please; the only opinions that matter to us are those of our leader and the foreign governments that sponsor him." If so, it is all the more difficult to imagine how international solidarity could possibly change the situation for those persecuted by the servants of darkness for leaving physical holes in the bodies of these servants’ colleagues.

It is equally unrealistic to imagine sending money or humanitarian aid to Ukrainian prisons without some corrupt arrangement with the administration; even the relatives of an ordinary prisoner—someone not labeled as an "enemy of the state"—must regularly pay fees just to ensure that a parcel actually reaches the addressee. It is hardly surprising that European Stalinists—who have been holding rallies for several years now to support the Kononovich brothers and other their comrades persecuted by Ukraine—do not really engage in this kind of activity. On the other hand, the mere fact that certain prisoners of social war are known by name abroad, and that their fates are being monitored internationally, can make it significantly more difficult for the dictatorship to kill them in prison or cause irreparable damage to their health. However, given the regime’s drive to a total blackout on any information about such people, it is highly likely that their fate will remain unknown, regardless of what happens to them. And this means that solidarity actions with them will quite possibly have an initially unclear outcome.

So, our role is to provide you with news; how you choose to use it—after weighing all the pros and cons—is entirely up to you. We also recognize that most of our audience consumes our content quite selectively: Ukrainian readers are interested mostly in applied advises, while the foreign public focuses mostly on an ideological agenda, disregarding any facts that do not fit into a black-and-white, "fascist state vs. anti-fascist society" framework. There is no other way to explain why, even in late 2026, some European anarchists continue to declare "solidarity with Ukrainian draft dodgers" as if this is an anti-war political movement with a unified goal—ignoring the reality that, with the tightening of Ukraine’s state policy since 2023–2024, the ranks of those evading the draft have been literally flooded with adherents of various right-wing ideologies, ranging from officious OUN-inspired anti-Russian chauvinism to the more subcultural NS/WP underground. Is not it absurd to stand in political solidarity with those who would likely wish them dead for rejecting Ukraine’s national borders or a transnational brotherhood of white men? While no fan of Bandera, Trump, or Milei is pre-programmed to remain him for life, it is equally obvious to us that blind glorification—based solely on the fact that someone is violating military registration rules—will never lead them to abandon their idols. The only thing capable of achieving that is exposing the contradictions between such positions and daily practice—a task our website carries out on a regular basis. Without this, the rhetoric of the typical Ukrainian regarding why he does not want to serve will remain at the level of "Let someone from another part of Ukraine do this," or "The drug-addicted Jew, acting on orders from globalists, is genociding the native population to replace us with colorful occupiers." Ukraine is currently a laboratory for Western ruling classes, where the most advanced methods for controlling and coercing the working class are being tested. The defeat and abolition of this slave pen is in the direct interest of everyone abroad who does not wish to have the same system imposed upon them.

It is all so complex, yet at the same time, so simple. For a war that has dragged on for nearly five years—one of the most senseless wars in world history—there are no anarchist solutions other than for soldiers to fraternize in the trenches, then head back—weapons in hand—to the government districts (or at least to their own homes), which first requires loosening up the rear so that the ground burns beneath the feet of the death cult sacrificers. The least you can do to help is to support us for shifting public opinion in this direction.
